title: Cosmic Optical and Infrared Backgrounds, Galaxy Counts and Surface-Brightness Bounds

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Settle in.
paragraphs: Welcome in. I am Professor Marek Nagy, and this is Cosmic Optical and Infrared Backgrounds, Galaxy Counts and Surface-Brightness Bounds. This is lesson 1 of 1 in the full thirty-minute build of this class. In this lesson we take the class's own material in order — nothing here is imported, and nothing is asked later that is not taught here first. We begin here: Settle in.

Settle in. I am Professor Marek Nagy, and this is Cosmic Optical and Infrared Backgrounds, Galaxy Counts and Surface-Brightness Bounds. This class is built on real papers — deposited, citable work. I will present each paper and what it reports; that presentation is the lesson. At the end I will ask you questions on what was taught here — nothing else.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

'A Baryon Budget for the Near-Infrared Excess: What a First-Stars Explanation Would Cost'. Its stated result: Computed budget study (2601 words). Headline computed values: I for fstar 0.001 nW = 0.2866; I for fstar 0.01 nW = 2.866; f star needed for 12nW = 0.04188; f star needed frac of baryons pct = 4.188; observed stellar baryon frac today pct = 6.
Now we go one step further into the material.

'Counts in an Expanding Volume: The Departure of the Count Slope from the Euclidean Value'. Its stated result: Computed budget study (2619 words). Headline computed values: cosmo count ratio 25 to 24 = 1.959; euclidean ratio per mag = 3.981; cosmo slope 24 25 dex per mag = 0.2919; cosmo slope 25 26 dex per mag = 0.2498. Verified against the public records API: exact title, state done, sole creator William Alexander Aldred with ORCID 0009-0000-1215-577X, CC BY 4.0 licence, and all four deposited files present.
The next piece is where this starts to come together.

'Diffuse Light Inside Halos: How Much Background Could Intrahalo Stars Supply?'. Its stated result: Computed budget study (2597 words). Headline computed values: I diffuse f0.10 nW = 0.8778; I diffuse f0.20 nW = 1.975; I diffuse f0.30 nW = 3.386; f needed for residual 5.56nW = 0.4131. Verified against the public records API: exact title, state done, sole creator William Alexander Aldred with ORCID 0009-0000-1215-577X, CC BY 4.0 licence, and all four deposited files present.
Listen carefully here — this piece carries weight in the questions later.

'Faint Near-Infrared Counts Beyond the Hubble Reach: How Much Extra Light Would a JWST Excess Supply?'. Its stated result: Computed budget study (2733 words). Headline computed values: extra counts per deg2 28 31 = 1.232e+06; extra light nW = 0.06036; base light 28 31 nW = 0.0427; extra frac of band light = 1.414; extra frac of total ebl 15nW = 0.004024; counts per arcmin2 at 30 hst = 87.47; counts per arcmin2 at 30 jwst = 227.4.
We take the pieces in order, because each one stands on the last.

'Our Own Galaxy's Scattered Light: A Cirrus-Traced Budget for Diffuse Galactic Contamination of the Background'. Its stated result: Computed budget study (2630 words). Headline computed values: DGL at 1MJy nW = 4; DGL at 2MJy nW = 8; residual at 1MJy nW = 0.8; residual frac of ebl at 1MJy = 0.08; I100 max for residual below 1nW = 1.25. Verified against the public records API: exact title, state done, sole creator William Alexander Aldred with ORCID 0009-0000-1215-577X, CC BY 4.0 licence, and all four deposited files present.
Stay with me, because the next piece builds directly on that one.

'Resolved and Unresolved Far-Infrared Light: The Fraction of the 250-Micron Background in Counted Sources'. Its stated result: Computed budget study (2627 words). Headline computed values: total CIB 250um nW model = 10; resolved frac above 0.005Jy = 0.7538; resolved frac above 0.01Jy = 0.6427; resolved frac above 0.02Jy = 0.4994; resolved frac above 0.05Jy = 0.2745; resolved frac above 0.1Jy = 0.1186; confusion cut Jy = 0.02.
Here is the next piece of the material, in the order the class presents it.

Now my worked example — this class's set problem, worked in full. The problem: Take the paper “A Baryon Budget for the Near-Infrared Excess: What a First-Stars Explanation Would Cost”. Its stated result is: Computed budget study (2601 words). Headline computed values: I for fstar 0.001 nW = 0.2866; I for fstar 0.01 nW = 2.866; f star needed for 12nW = 0.04188; f star needed frac of baryons pct = 4.188; observed stellar baryon frac today pct = 6. (a) Restate the claim in your own words. (b) Name one observation or computation that could prove it wrong. The worked answer: A strong answer restates the claim without borrowing the paper’s wording, then names a test the paper itself would accept — here, the natural test is to recompute or re-measure the headline quantity in the stated result and check it against the paper’s own number, under the paper’s own stated assumptions.

Let us gather what this lesson taught, in order: Settle in; 'A Baryon Budget for the Near-Infrared Excess: What a First-Stars Explanation Would Cost'; 'Counts in an Expanding Volume: The Departure of the Count Slope from the Euclidean Value'; 'Diffuse Light Inside Halos: How Much Background Could Intrahalo Stars Supply?'; 'Faint Near-Infrared Counts Beyond the Hubble Reach: How Much Extra Light Would a JWST Excess Supply?'; 'Our Own Galaxy's Scattered Light: A Cirrus-Traced Budget for Diffuse Galactic Contamination of the Background'. Those are the pieces — hold them in that order, because the questions follow the same road.

That is the lesson, whole. Below it are the questions — every one of them drawn from what was just taught, and nothing else. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read a piece again is learning, not cheating. When you are ready, begin.

questions.teach: Think back to the lesson — the paper 'A Baryon Budget for the Near-Infrared Excess: What a First-Stars Explanation Would Cost'. The result it reported gives a value for nW, and that value is what this question asks for.
questions.teach2: Here is the exact passage from the lesson again: 'A Baryon Budget for the Near-Infrared Excess: What a First-Stars Explanation Would Cost'. And here is that same result with the words stripped away — just the quantities standing in a row: nW = 0.2866; star needed for 12nW = 0.04188; frac of baryons pct = 4.188. Find nW in that row; the value beside it is the one this question asks for. Say it in figures, any honest form: as printed, rounded, or written out in full.
questions.walk: Walk it through with me, step by step. (1) In the lesson, the paper 'A Baryon Budget for the Near-Infrared Excess: What a First-Stars Explanation Would Cost' stated its result. (4) In that row, nW stands beside 0.2866 — so the answer the lesson gives is 0.2866. Now it is yours: say that value, in any honest form.
